newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Balkan laggards hope for foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Balkan laggards hope for foreign investment.

text.p: As their more prosperous neighbours limber up to join the European Union, Balkan states who missed the first wave of post-1989 investment are trying with varying degrees of success to woo investors now.

Once-isolated Romania started far behind the other two seven years ago but now boasts falling unemployment and the discipline imposed by an International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme, plus a bigger potential market than the other two combined.
Bulgaria finally got reforms under way this year, but foreign investors looking at Yugoslavia say political and economic risks in Serbia and Montenegro are still too high.

An outer wall of sanctions left in place after war-related United Nations controls were lifted last October bar Belgrade's return to the IMF and other international bodies, constituting a key obstacle to any significant foreign capital inflow.

The removal of sanctions is conditional on a range of political requirements including implementing the Dayton peace accord for Bosnia, cooperation with the Hague war crimes tribunal, respect for human rights and further democratisation.

"If you invest in Yugoslavia, you're betting on when it's going to be rehabilitated with the IMF and resume repayments on its foreign debt," said Andrew Kenningham, fixed income strategist with Merrill Lynch.
"The economy is in the worst state of the three from the macro-economic point of view, and it's the most opaque, there's no information even on the level of reserves in the national bank."
LOCATION IS EVERYTHING
The strategic geo-political location of the three states at a crossroads between Western Europe, the former Soviet republics and the Middle East should make them attractive to foreign investors.

But anyone wanting to do business there must struggle with bureaucracy and a legal framework ill-adapted to their needs. In Bulgaria the threat of organised crime and racketeering is a deterrent, while protesting Romanian miners sacked the capital twice in the early 1990s and threatened to return last month.
BANKING SECTOR IS KEY INDICATOR
Romania's banking system is the healthiest of the three and the government is seeking strategic foreign investors to privatise some of the 42 banks in the fast-growing sector.
In Bulgaria, lax supervision of the country's numerous and illiquid banks helped create the conditions for last year's dramatic economic collapse.

Courts have declared five banks insolvent and the licence of a sixth has been withdrawn. Insolvency suits against another eight are pending. The reformist government's rescue plan envisions privatising six state banks by mid-1998.
Yugoslavia's 111 banks together posted a $12.5 million loss in 1996, with unrecoverable claims growing to $600 million.
The government has promised help but has opted to consolidate the banks into state-owned banking groups like the Beogradska Banka group established in May.
Romania and Bulgaria recently elected reformist governments which are trying to catch up with measures well advanced in other ex-communist countries.

Bulgaria is paying the price of more than seven years of lip service to reform but bankers say they are optimistic that the government which took office in May has the political will to carry out potentially unpopular measures such as closing and restructuring loss-making state firms.
A currency board regime has pegged the lev to the mark since July 1 and Prime Minister Ivan Kostov's latest proposal is to remove a ban on foreign investors buying land.

Investment so far has concentrated on short-term opportunities such as government debt, which earlier this year was offering high yields with the security of the lev peg. "But you've got to have the hot money go in first to put a place like this on the map," said a Sofia-based Western banker.

Romania and Bulgaria are following similar IMF-prescribed programmes, but Romania's government elected last November has a head start over its smaller southern neighbour in privatisation and closure of loss-making state firms.

Romania operates a stock exchange in Bucharest which trades 46 companies, as well as an over-the-counter market, where the number of listings stands at more than 3,000. The arrival of portfolio investors this year significantly increased volumes.
Bulgaria hopes to revive its bourse later this year.

A Romanian government decree on foreign investment giving tax breaks to investors and setting portfolio investment laws cleared parliament this month. In March, parliament passed a law allowing foreign ownership of land.

Romania hopes the legal reforms will combine with political stability, geographic location and cheap labour to reverse a decline in capital inflows. Foreign investment since 1989 has totalled $2.3 billion to date, compared to $1.098 billion in Bulgaria, official figures show.
